Compare the two side by side. (2) Confirm the cast differs from the 13 earlier heroes and H-0. (3) Confirm no needles or blood are visible at the access arm.

title: Adaptation: a process, not a stage
placement: Module 14, section `adaptation` (Adjusting to life on dialysis: losses, tasks, and sources of strength); the process idea is introduced in `model` (A life rearranged three times a week)
job: U/P — the learner sees adaptation as a path that loops back when life changes, and knows what losses, tasks, and strengths to look for.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold C, horizontal path with loop-backs)
alt: Adaptation to dialysis drawn as a winding path from shock and grief to working acceptance, with life events that send the patient back, and the tasks and strengths that help.
caption: Most patients move back and forth between shock, grief, anger, bargaining, resignation, and a working acceptance, and they move again when something changes. A patient who seemed settled for two years can be in crisis this month.
reviewer_flags: The six emotional states are drawn as places on a path, not as fixed stages in order; the text lists them without a sequence. Confirm the wording "working acceptance".

title: From screen to referral: what happens next
placement: Module 14, section `screening` (Screening for depression, anxiety, and related problems, and what happens next)
job: A — the learner can give a screening questionnaire safely and knows exactly what each kind of result triggers, including the crisis branch.
skill: williamriveromd-algorithm-generator-skill (Style Mode C, house style)
alt: Screening pathway: check the patient is alert and stable, explain and give privacy, then report a positive score the same day, act at once on any self-harm answer, and report concern even after a negative screen.
caption: A score is a screen, not a diagnosis. A positive answer about death or self-harm overrides the total score, and a questionnaire never overrules a nurse's own worry. A referral that is never completed helps no one, so ask at the next session.
reviewer_flags: (1) Module flag: content on depression and suicide risk needs review by a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist with dialysis experience before release. (2) No thresholds, intervals, or hotline numbers appear; the National Center for Mental Health hotline (1553) is stated in the text but is left out of the figure because the text asks that the number and hours be checked before giving it. Confirm.

title: Delirium, depression, or dementia?
placement: Module 14, section `physiology` (How kidney failure and dialysis affect mood, thinking, sleep, and behavior)
job: A — the learner can tell the three conditions apart by onset, course, and attention, and knows that a new change in alertness is treated as delirium.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold E reference card)
alt: Delirium, depression, and dementia compared by onset, course, attention, typical causes in dialysis patients, and nursing response; delirium is an emergency until explained.
caption: A new change in alertness or attention is treated as delirium, and therefore as a physical problem, until a physician has assessed it. The three conditions can occur together, and each makes the others harder to recognize.
reviewer_flags: none

title: De-escalation, step by step
placement: Module 14, section `deescalation` (De-escalation, step by step)
job: A — the learner can run the eight de-escalation steps in order, starting with safety and a check of the body, and knows what not to do.
skill: williamriveromd-algorithm-generator-skill (Style Mode C, house style; vertical step ladder)
alt: Eight de-escalation steps from safety and space and a body check to setting limits and knowing when to stop, with a list of what not to do.
caption: Check the body before judging the person: a glucose, a blood pressure, and an oxygen saturation take less than two minutes. Stopping treatment, restraint, sedation, or transfer are physician decisions under facility policy, never a nurse's improvised response.
reviewer_flags: Unit policy names who is called and how security is summoned; the figure says "per policy" only. Confirm.

title: Exercise on dialysis, and the most dangerous hour for a fall
placement: Module 14, section `exercise` (Muscle, movement, and exercise on dialysis); also supports `frailty-falls` (Frailty, orthostatic hypotension, and falls)
job: A — the learner can apply the safety screen before exercise during treatment and the end-of-session steps that prevent falls.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold B, two-panel comparison with a shared takeaway bar)
alt: Left, the safety screen before exercise during dialysis with reasons not to start or to stop; right, the post-dialysis hour with sitting up, standing with support, and home fall-prevention tips.
caption: Exercise makes patients stronger and helps them walk farther and stay independent; trials have not shown that it lowers mortality. The hour after dialysis is the most dangerous time of the week for a fall, so rise in stages and report repeated dizziness.
reviewer_flags: The text gives trial results (for example 1,211 patients, 3.85 repetitions); the figure states only the direction ("stronger, not proven to lengthen life") to keep it readable. Confirm.

title: Symptom burden and recovery time: ask, rate, report, recheck
placement: Module 14, section `symptoms` (Symptom burden: asking routinely and reporting for treatment)

skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold D, hub-and-spoke with a loop)
alt: The recovery-time question at the center of seven common dialysis symptoms, with a loop from asking and rating to reporting, treatment by the physician, rechecking, and telling the patient.
caption: "How long does it take you to recover from a dialysis session?" A recovery time of more than 12 hours has been associated with poorer quality of life and higher risks of hospitalization and death. A questionnaire that is filed and never acted on teaches patients not to bother answering.
reviewer_flags: "Associated with" wording kept; the figure does not imply that shortening recovery time prevents death. Confirm.

caption: none (hero vignette; the page title sits beside it).
reviewer_flags: (1) Module 1's hero also shows a weighing scale (column scale beside a seated man having his blood pressure taken); this hero differs in action (patient standing on the scale), ward, camera, and cast. Confirm they read as different scenes. (2) Edema must be visible but not grotesque.

title: The glomerular filtration barrier: how a living filter holds, leaks, or bleeds
placement: Module 15, section `physiology` (The filtration barrier, immune injury, and why the complications follow)
job: U — the learner can name the three layers of the barrier, sees that podocytes are the final barrier to albumin, and recognizes what changes in a leaking versus an inflamed glomerulus.
skill: williamriveromd-biomedical-mechanism-figure
alt: Three layers of the glomerular filter, capillary lining, basement membrane, and podocytes with slit diaphragms, shown healthy, leaking albumin when foot processes flatten, and bleeding red cells when inflamed.
caption: Blood is separated from urine by three layers that work together. When podocyte foot processes flatten, albumin escapes (the nephrotic pattern); when immune attack damages the capillary wall, red cells escape and filtration falls (the nephritic pattern).
reviewer_flags: Schematic simplification: mesangium, Bowman capsule detail, and crescents are not drawn. Confirm.

title: Leak or bleed: nephrotic and nephritic patterns compared
placement: Module 15, section `model` (A living filter that can leak or bleed); also supports `nephrotic` and `nephritic`
job: U/A — the learner can sort a presentation into the leak or the bleed pattern and knows the main danger and the nursing watch for each.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold B comparison)
alt: Nephrotic and nephritic patterns compared: urine, blood tests, swelling, blood pressure, kidney function, main dangers, and typical diseases, with a note that real patients can show a mixture.
caption: The two patterns are a starting point for thinking, not a diagnosis; lupus, for example, can leak and bleed at once. The diagnosis usually needs blood tests and often a kidney biopsy.
reviewer_flags: "Above 3.5 g per day" is the KDIGO 2021 definition as quoted in m15.py `evidence`. Confirm that you want it on the figure; delete the line if not.

title: Kidney biopsy: the nursing timeline
placement: Module 15, section `biopsy` (Kidney biopsy: nursing care before, during, and after)
job: A — the learner can prepare a patient for biopsy, observe afterward against the pre-biopsy baseline, and recognize bleeding to report at once.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold C, horizontal timeline with an alert band)
alt: Kidney biopsy nursing timeline: checks before, positioning and specimens during, bed rest and observation after, discharge teaching, and a red-flag band of bleeding signs to report at once.
caption: The main risk of a kidney biopsy is bleeding. Most bleeds are small and stop by themselves; careful preparation and close observation in the first hours keep small bleeds small and catch large ones early.
reviewer_flags: Bed-rest length and observation intervals are "per protocol" in the text; the figure shows no hours. Confirm.

title: Immunosuppressive medicines: the nurse's watch-list
placement: Module 15, section `immunosuppression` (Glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive medicines: what the nurse watches)
job: A — the learner knows what to check before the first dose and what to watch, teach, and report for each medicine used in glomerular disease.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold E reference card with a checklist column)
alt: Watch-list card for glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate, rituximab, calcineurin inhibitors, and hydroxychloroquine, with a before-the-first-dose safety checklist and teaching for life on immunosuppression.
caption: The benefits and the main dangers of these medicines come from the same action, damping the immune system. The nurse never starts, stops, or adjusts them, but checks, teaches, and reports, and may hold a dose and call when the protocol says so.
reviewer_flags: (1) Overlaps in part with 11-C (transplant immunosuppressant card) from the first brief; this card is specific to glomerular disease (cyclophosphamide, rituximab, hydroxychloroquine, the pre-treatment checklist). Confirm both are wanted. (2) Drug names are generic names as written in the text; no brand names. (3) Dense; if the six rows garble after two tries, keep the checklist column as the image and leave the table to the HTML.

title: Polycystic kidney disease runs in families: one chance in two
placement: Module 15, section `diabetic-pkd` (Diabetic kidney disease, when it may not be diabetic, and polycystic kidney disease)
job: U/A — the learner can explain one-in-two inheritance in plain words and carry out the nurse's family-screening steps with respect for choice and confidentiality.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold B, family tree plus action steps)
alt: Family tree showing that each child of a parent with polycystic kidney disease has a one-in-two chance of inheriting the gene, with the nurse's five family-screening steps and key teaching points.
caption: Each child of an affected parent has a one-in-two chance of inheriting the gene, and the chance is the same for every child. A relative who carries the gene can still benefit from early blood pressure control and kidney protection.
reviewer_flags: The family tree is illustrative (one affected parent, four children, two affected); real families vary, and the figure says "the chance is the same for every child". Confirm that showing two of four affected does not mislead; an alternative is a single coin-toss icon per child with no outcome drawn.

title: Present at the chair

title: Two tracks that run side by side

reviewer_flags: The endpoint of the supportive track is drawn as a soft sunrise-colored band labeled "End-of-life care: comfort, family close", with no death imagery. Confirm.

title: The symptom wheel: assess, comfort, report

job: A — the learner can run the same assess-comfort-report pattern for each common symptom and knows the medicine-safety warning signs in kidney failure.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold D, wheel with a center and an outer safety ring)
alt: Symptom wheel with eight segments, pain, itch, breathlessness, nausea and appetite, fatigue, restlessness, low mood, and sleep, each with the nursing comfort measure, around the steps ask, rate, comfort, report, and reassess.

title: Advance care planning: a conversation in steps
placement: Module 16, section `acp` (Advance care planning: goals, a trusted voice, and a written record)
job: A — the learner knows the seven steps of advance care planning, which are the nurse's and which are the physician's, and how to work with Filipino family and faith.

alt: Seven advance care planning steps from opening the topic to reviewing the plan, each with the nurse's part, plus a band on Filipino family and faith and a note that facility policy governs written plans.

reviewer_flags: The legal line reflects the module's statement that no Philippine advance-directive law was verified at the time of writing; re-check before publishing.

title: When a patient asks to stop dialysis: the screening and team pathway
placement: Module 16, section `withdrawal` (When a patient asks to stop dialysis)
job: A — the learner can respond to a request to stop dialysis by listening, screening for depression and suicide risk, looking for reversible causes, bringing in the team, and ensuring care continues after a decision.
skill: williamriveromd-algorithm-generator-skill (Style Mode C, house style)
alt: Pathway after a request to stop dialysis: listen, screen mood and safety, look for reversible causes, inform the nephrologist the same day, capacity assessment and family meeting with options, then respect the decision and continue care.

reviewer_flags: (1) Sensitive content; review with the medical director and, where available, the palliative care team. (2) No survival times are shown (the text gives study figures in `physiology`); this pathway avoids them deliberately. Confirm.

title: The marked bottle

title: A narrow doorway into a large room: working memory and chunking
placement: Module 17, section `physiology` (The science of learning and memory in a person with kidney disease); the analogy is introduced in `model` (A narrow doorway into a large room)
job: U — the learner sees why long lists are forgotten, how familiar bundles (chunks) pass the doorway, and what narrows it in kidney disease.
skill: williamriveromd-biomedical-mechanism-figure (concept schematic with a worked example strip)
alt: Working memory drawn as a narrow doorway into the large room of long-term memory: a list of ten instructions jams at the door, while two or three familiar bundles pass through; fear, pain, poor sleep, and noise narrow the doorway.
caption: Adults can hold only about four meaningful chunks in mind at once. Two or three points per session, linked to what the patient already knows, pass the doorway; retrieval through teach-back and repetition across sessions keep them easy to find.
reviewer_flags: none

title: The teach-back loop
placement: Module 17, section `bedside` (Teaching in the dialysis chair); also supports `teaching-plan`
job: A — the learner can run teach-back as a loop that checks the teacher, re-explains differently when there is a gap, and documents learning, then repeats at the next session.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold D, cycle with a decision point)
alt: Teach-back loop: choose the moment, teach one goal in two or three points, ask the patient to explain in their own words, re-explain differently if there is a gap, document the learning, and ask again next session.
caption: Teach-back checks the teacher; it is never an examination of the patient. If the answer has a gap, re-explain in a different way, not louder and not in the same words, and ask again; then ask once more at the next session.
reviewer_flags: none

title: Absolute or relative? The DAPA-CKD worked example in 100 people
placement: Module 17, section `reading-evidence` (Questions to ask of a study or a guideline)
job: A — the learner can compute and explain absolute risk reduction, relative risk reduction, and number needed to treat from the module's worked example, and see why starting risk changes the absolute benefit.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold B, paired icon arrays with a worked-arithmetic strip)
alt: Two grids of 100 people: 14.5 had the main outcome with placebo and 9.2 with dapagliflozin; about 5 fewer per 100, a 37% relative reduction, and about 19 treated to prevent one event.
caption: A relative reduction sounds the same whatever a patient's starting risk; the absolute benefit depends on it. When explaining benefit to patients, say the absolute figure as a frequency: "about 5 in 100 people."
reviewer_flags: (1) Icon arrays cannot show decimals with whole icons; the figure shades one icon half (14.5) and one icon about one-fifth (9.2), with the decimal printed beside each grid. If the generator cannot shade partial icons cleanly after two tries, change the arrays to 1,000 small dots (145 versus 92) or use the HTML table. (2) The hypothetical low-risk panel is labeled "Hypothetical, not trial data" as in the text.

title: The evidence-based practice cycle, with PICO spelled out
placement: Module 17, section `ebp` (Evidence-based practice: from a question at the chair to a shared result)
job: A — the learner can turn a unit worry into a PICO question, move through the five steps, and tell when a project has become research that needs ethics review.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold D, cycle with a worked PICO table)
alt: Evidence-based practice cycle: ask a PICO question, search, appraise, apply with judgment and the patient, and evaluate locally, then share; with a worked PICO for fluid teaching and a research-or-improvement checkpoint.
caption: Evidence-based practice combines the best current evidence with clinical expertise and the patient's values. A change in a nursing routine goes through the nurse manager; any change to treatment needs an order; and work designed to produce knowledge beyond the unit needs ethics review before it starts.
reviewer_flags: none

title: The Filipino plate on a dialysis day
placement: Module 3, section `hd-meals` (Filipino meals on dialysis days); also supports `hd-nutrition` (How eating changes once hemodialysis starts)
job: A — the learner can coach a patient on HD to build a familiar plate with more protein, less salt, and lower-potassium choices, and to count sabaw as fluid.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold B, plate diagram with swap cards)
alt: A Filipino dialysis-day plate with measured rice, a palm-sized portion of fish or egg, and a lower-potassium vegetable, with swaps for salty and processed foods, a small cup of sabaw counted as fluid, and the binder taken with the first spoonful.
caption: On hemodialysis, protein needs go up while salt, potassium, and phosphate still count every day. Change the portion, the preparation, or one ingredient at a time, starting from what the patient ate yesterday; the renal dietitian sets the individual plan.
reviewer_flags: (1) Distinct from 03-C (Filipino food guide by nutrient) in the first brief; this figure is the dialysis-day plate and swaps. Confirm both are wanted. (2) Portion sizes are relative ("measured", "palm-sized"); no grams or cups are shown. The renal dietitian should confirm the plate proportions.

title: A cough at the door: tuberculosis triage in an open unit
placement: Module 7, section `tb` (Tuberculosis in the dialysis unit); also supports `respiratory` (Respiratory-virus seasons in the unit)
job: A — the learner can screen at the door, mask and separate a coughing patient at once, and apply the physician's airborne-precaution plan in a unit with no isolation room.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold B, floor plan with a step sequence)
alt: Floor plan of an open dialysis unit with the coughing patient masked and seated at the far station near an exhaust fan, staff in fitted respirators, beside the steps from screening at the door to the physician's plan.

Where and when the patient is dialyzed, and when precautions end, are decided by the physician and the infection-control officer; tuberculosis is not spread through the blood circuit, so standard machine cleaning applies.
reviewer_flags: No national rule for placing a suspected TB patient in an open unit was verified (module quiz flag); the floor plan shows the text's options "per the unit's written plan". Confirm against the unit's plan.

title: The unit vaccination record, and the hepatitis B decision path

title: The monthly panel: draw it right, read the trend, act

title: Glucose on a dialysis day
placement: Module 9, section `diabetes-hd` (Diabetes on hemodialysis: why glucose behaves differently)
job: U/A — the learner can explain why glucose behaves differently on HD, anticipate low readings after the session, sample from the right site, and distrust a reassuring HbA1c.

title: Pregnancy on dialysis: the shared care map

title: A child is not a small adult

title: Professional boundaries: seven situations, seven responses
placement: Module 12, section `conduct` (Professional conduct: boundaries, privacy, handoff, and speaking up)
job: A — the learner can match common boundary situations in long-term dialysis care to the professional response.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold E, scenario cards)
alt: Seven scenario cards, a cash gift, a photo on social media, a corridor handoff, a supplier's gift, false audit records, a senior nurse ridiculing a new nurse, and a herbal tea, each paired with the professional response.
caption: Warmth toward patients is part of good care; a personal or financial relationship is not. Covering for a colleague is not loyalty, and cultural humility means asking about a remedy without ridicule.
reviewer_flags: Scenario wording is shortened to fit the cards; confirm the shortened responses.

alt: A waterproof dialysis emergency bag laid out with its contents: the dialysis information card, medicine list and reserve, emergency-diet foods and a measured cup, flashlight, power bank, and cash, plus extra items for diabetes and for peritoneal dialysis.

title: Plasma exchange: spinning or sieving the plasma out
placement: Module 13, section `tpe-principles` (Therapeutic plasma exchange: removing what no dialyzer can)
job: U — the learner sees how plasma exchange differs from dialysis and how centrifugal and membrane machines separate plasma, what is removed, and what replaces it.
skill: williamriveromd-biomedical-mechanism-figure, with dialysis-circuit-schematic port rules for the membrane panel (end caps blood only, side ports fluid only, infusions as short stubs)
alt: Centrifugal and membrane plasma separation compared: a spinning chamber layers cells outward and draws plasma off, and a plasma filter lets plasma through its pores; removed plasma goes to waste and albumin or donor plasma is returned with the cells.
caption: A dialyzer keeps proteins in the blood; plasma exchange removes the plasma itself, with the antibodies and other large proteins dissolved in it, and replaces it. Neither separation method has been shown to be better for patients in general.
reviewer_flags: (1) The text does not say where the replacement fluid joins the circuit; the figure joins it to the return (blue) line after the separator in both panels, following the house rule that an infusion joins the blood line as a short stub. Confirm against the apheresis service's machines. (2) The membrane filter's upper side port is drawn capped because there is no dialysate in plasma exchange; some plasma filters have one filtrate port only. (3) No blood flows, volumes, or exchange amounts appear.

title: During plasma exchange: citrate, low calcium, and the other reactions

alt: Plasma exchange watch algorithm: checks before the session, then early and late signs of citrate-related low calcium, low blood pressure, allergic reaction to plasma, and bleeding, each with first actions and reporting, and the record after the session.
caption: Early citrate symptoms are things the patient feels, so a patient taught to say "tingling" at once is the first alarm. The nurse watches the patient more than the machine and acts per order and protocol; severe signs are an emergency.
